clinicalPearls: Out-toeing is less common than in-toeing and, like it, is usually a benign rotational variant
In early infancy a bilateral out-toeing is often due to an external rotation contracture of the hip from intrauterine positioning, which resolves once the child bears weight and walks
In older children external tibial torsion and femoral retroversion are the usual causes, and external tibial torsion tends to increase rather than diminish with growth
The level of the deformity is defined by a rotational profile using the foot progression angle, hip rotation, and the thigh-foot angle
External tibial torsion may combine with a valgus knee to aggravate patellofemoral maltracking and anterior knee pain in adolescence
New or unilateral out-toeing in an older or overweight child should raise concern for a slipped capital femoral epiphysis, in which the limb externally rotates
Most physiological out-toeing needs only reassurance and observation, with surgery reserved for severe, symptomatic, persistent deformity
reference.pathophysiology: Out-toeing describes an outwardly directed foot progression angle during walking, produced by external rotational alignment at the hip, tibia, or foot. In the infant it commonly reflects a residual external rotation contracture of the hip capsule from intrauterine position, which stretches out with ambulation. In the older child it usually arises from external tibial torsion or reduced femoral anteversion (relative retroversion), representing variation in the normal course of skeletal derotation. Unlike internal torsion, external tibial torsion often progresses with growth. Pathological out-toeing is important to recognise because hip disorders such as a slipped capital femoral epiphysis characteristically hold the limb in external rotation.
additionalDifferentials: Femoral retroversion or reduced femoral anteversion
External rotation contracture of the hip in infancy
Slipped capital femoral epiphysis in the older child
additionalInvestigations: Full rotational profile with foot progression angle, hip rotation, and thigh-foot angle
Observation of gait for symmetry and pattern
Examination of the hips for restricted internal rotation suggesting a slipped epiphysis
Hip radiographs including a frog-lateral view when a slipped capital femoral epiphysis is suspected
Assessment of the feet for planovalgus or calcaneovalgus deformity
Standing lower-limb radiographs where associated angular deformity is present
redFlags: New or unilateral out-toeing in an older or overweight child suggesting a slipped capital femoral epiphysis
Hip or knee pain, limp, or restricted hip internal rotation
Progressive external tibial torsion with worsening patellofemoral symptoms
Neurological signs indicating an underlying neuromuscular disorder
reference.prognosis: Physiological out-toeing generally carries a good prognosis, with infantile hip contractures resolving after walking begins; external tibial torsion is less predictable and may persist or progress, occasionally warranting correction for symptoms.
pitfalls: Dismissing unilateral out-toeing in an adolescent and missing a slipped capital femoral epiphysis
Assuming out-toeing always resolves, when external tibial torsion can worsen with growth
Failing to localise the deformity with a rotational profile
Overtreating benign infantile out-toeing with unnecessary orthoses
Overlooking associated patellofemoral maltracking that may need attention
references: Staheli LT, rotational problems of the lower extremity
management: Reassure and observe physiological out-toeing, as infantile hip external-rotation contractures resolve once weight-bearing and walking begin
Serial monitoring of the rotational profile, including foot progression angle, hip rotation and thigh-foot angle, to track the natural course
Reserve derotational tibial osteotomy for severe, persistent external tibial torsion causing symptoms or patellofemoral maltracking
Conservative management of associated planovalgus foot deformity and anterior knee pain
Urgently exclude and manage a slipped capital femoral epiphysis in a new or unilateral out-toeing older or overweight child, with frog-lateral hip radiographs and prompt orthopaedic referral
Refer to paediatric orthopaedics when the deformity is unilateral, progressive, painful or outside the expected developmental pattern
